newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Gun law muddies hopes of peace in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Gun law muddies hopes of peace in Tajikistan.

text.p: Checkpoints show who holds what in the fractious former Soviet republic of Tajikistan -- the government, Islamist opposition guerrillas or simply highway robbers.
Along the country's few passable roads, the signal to stop is a burst from a Kalashnikov assault rifle, fired into the air.
After four years of civil war in which thousands were killed, a ceasefire has now held for seven months in the remote republic wedged between Afghanistan and China.
The government and its armed Islamist enemy plan to sign a peace accord in Moscow on Friday.
But the conflict has left Tajikistan awash with weapons. And with the economy shattered, the gun and the checkpoint are the quickest way to make money.
"The roads are controlled by all sorts of criminal groups," said one diplomat.
"None of our factories is working," complained a local government official in Kofarnikhon 20 km (12 miles) east of the capital Dushanbe. "Now all we have is what we grow in the fields."

Inside a government building is a faded propaganda poster of a barrel-chested Soviet-era shockworker clutching a spanner in front of factory chimneys, a reminder that Kofarnikhon was once a busy industrial city.
"We dream of peace," said the official, who asked not to be named. "But there are a few who don't want this. They see the easiest way to fill their stomachs is having a gun."
Under the peace accord, government troops and guerrillas must join a new national force or put down their weapons. But in Kofarnikhon, neither side seems ready to trust the other.
Earlier this month, violence was only narrowly avoided in the town after police detained two opposition fighters who had returned to visit their families.
"We don't talk to the guerrillas, they're not legal, though I have to write about the coming peace everyday," said Mirzo Faizali, editor of the official local newspaper Vakhdad (Unity).
City council chief Kurbanali Azimov had this message for any opposition fighters wanting to return: "If someone wants to come back and see their families, they're welcome. Only no guns."
A few km (miles) up the fast grey waters of the Kofarnikhon river in the scrub-covered mountains of the Romit valley, an opposition guerrilla, one hand clutching his rifle, disagreed.
"We have no guarantees, absolutely none," said Ismat Azizov, a bearded fighter in Soviet combat fatigues. "We have to carry these (guns) for self defence."
Azizov said he had slipped into Kofarnikhon to see his family but only felt safe for an hour or two: "But thanks to Allah it is better than before when I couldn't see them at all."

A home-made rocket launcher was propped in a corner of his unit's small shack, shaded by tall poplars next to the roaring river. Afghan hats hung from nails on the wall. Many guerrillas operated out of camps in Afghanistan during the civil war.
A fighter put down a large wooden bowl of "mujahedjski shurpa" (guerrilla stew) and poured tea for Azizov and the unit commander, Nozim Yusupov.

"We're not tired of war yet, we're used to it," said Yusupov, munching on a slice of watermelon. "If there was no war, we'd be bored," he said, sounding an ominous note for the negotiators gathering in Moscow to sign Friday's peace accord.
